newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Majority of Brazilians support police pay demands.
newsitem.headline: Majority of Brazilians support police pay demands.

text.p: A majority of Brazilians believe that military police are justified in staging protests to demand higher salaries, a survey published on Sunday said.
Military policemen have been protesting across the country in the last few weeks, on several occasions engaging in pitched battles with army troops.
The Datafolha poll found that 89 percent of respondents thought the police were justified in demanding better wages and 60 percent thought they should have a legal right to strike.
In the northeastern city of Recife, policemen deserted their posts last weekend, allowing thieves to run riot in the city centre, robbing pedestrians and looting shops.
Gen. Alberto Cardoso, head of the military office of the presidency, said the protests had dealt a death blow to the military police and signalled a total breakdown in discipline.

"The military police has been profoundly wounded, I would even say fatally wounded," Cardoso told daily newspaper O Globo in an interview published on Sunday. "It's logical that those responsible will have to answer for this."

But the recent rash of protests has helped to improve the popular image of Brazil's military police, notorious for brutality and frequent abuses of power, the survey in daily newspaper Folha de Sao Paulo found.

Forty percent of Sao Paulo residents said they trusted the military police more than they feared them, up from 24 percent in April when public confidence hit an all-time low in the wake of amateur videotapes showing officers beating civilians.
A majority thought the protesters were motivated by economic, rather than political, reasons and preferred peaceful marches to an all-out strike, the survey found.
The police protests have spread to the majority of Brazil's 27 states after the state government in Minas Gerais caved in to protesters last month and awarded them a 48.2 percent pay rise.
Datafolha interviewed 4,601 people on July 24 in 10 cities that have been affected by the disturbances.
